    #148377. Industry News: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2100 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself.
    • It has been revealed that at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result.
    • Recent findings suggest that and then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of Fresh England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us.”.

    It has been revealed that at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the Fresh England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Blueprint, the World Bank, and the currently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment, the juvenile death penalty (until 2005), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that and then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law.

    A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, in which the justices will review one of the Trump administration’s earliest attempts to restrict immigration. On the administration’s first day, a presidential proclamation declared that “an invasion is ongoing on the southern border.” The proclamation, among other things, sought to suspend entry to the United States for non-citizens “engaged in the invasion,” even for refugees fleeing persecution and seeking to apply for asylum. But the edict went one step further. It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.

    The proclamation was issued notwithstanding a congressional framework that seeks to facilitate asylum – indefinite lawful residence – to those escaping persecution in their home country, set forth primarily in the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by the 1980 Refugee Act and later amendments (codified under Title 8 of the U.S. Code). This framework: a) ensures a right to apply for asylum, b) links eligibility for asylum to refugee status, and c) provides protections against the government removing persons who would be likely to face persecution or torture.

    According to recent reports, section 1158 establishes the right to seek asylum. It provides that “[a]ny alien who is physically present in the United States … irrespective of such alien’s status, may apply for asylum.” The same section makes eligibility for asylum conditional, among other things, on a demonstration of refugee status. For this the statute relies on the definition of refugee in section 1101(a)(42) as a person who is unwilling or unable to return to their home country “because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”.

    In a recent development, in turn, safeguards from removal come from two sources. The immigration statute itself states that noncitizens cannot be removed to a country where the attorney general determines that the “alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” In addition, the Foreign Affairs Reform & Restructuring Act of 1998 restricts removal to a country when “there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.”.

    The Trump administration initially justified the denial of asylum and removal protections to those within the United States by invoking the president’s authority to suspend entry “of any aliens or of any class of aliens into the United States [that] would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The logic is that no one who violated the suspension by entering should be entitled to asylum and removal protections. To this defense the administration has added the formal role of the attorney general and director of Homeland Security. The INA grants each official the authority to grant asylum to eligible applicants as well as withhold removal for those who qualify. At the same time, the statute makes clear that these decisions are subject to individualized judicial review under an “abuse of discretion” standard. (At least until the second Trump administration, decisions not to grant relief to those who had demonstrated that they had qualified for asylum were the “exceedingly rare“ exception.).

    The lower courts rejected both justifications. Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the administration’s claim that the president’s suspension of entry to those “engaged in [the] invasion” invalidated asylum and removal protections that expressly applied to persons physically in the country. The D.C. Circuit agreed with a slightly different emphasis. Writing for the majority, Judge Michelle Childs also rejected the idea that a suspension of entry justified eliminating asylum and removal safeguards for those present in the United States. To this point she added that, as a grant of asylum is discretionary, the express right to apply it entails individualized consideration rather than blanket elimination. (Judge Justin Walker issued a partial dissenting argument that the grant of discretionary authority permits a blanket denial of asylum claims.).

    Recent findings suggest that the D.C. courts’ holdings are not wrong so far as they go. Suspending entry would appear to be a different power from removing someone after they had entered. The provisions for asylum strongly imply individualized consideration and even suggest a presumption of granting asylum to those who meet the detailed eligibility requirements. The relevant provisions plainly bar removal of those who qualify for that protection. But whether this reasoning will be sufficient at the Supreme Court is another matter. This is so not least given the justices’ recent penchant for giving the executive wide latitude on immigration.

    But the justices should take into account some additional perspective.

    One relevant perspective comes from international law. Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum. More surprising still, these common global challenges has yielded what should be familiar, common legal standards that apply, and to a great extent which owe their development to, the United States. Perhaps most surprising of all, standard domestic doctrines invite reference to this body of law when interpreting applicable federal statutes.

    Consider first asylum. As an initial matter, the domestic asylum framework incorporates international standards as a function of congressional intent. As the court itself recognized in 1987’s INS v. Cardozo-Fonseca, Congress enacted the Refugee Act of 1980 to bring U.S. law in conformity with the nation’s obligations as a state party to the 1967 Protocol to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Crucially, in determining those obligations, the court sensibly drew upon the views of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees.

    What do those obligations contemplate? The Refugee Conventions do not expressly provide for a right to apply for long-term asylum, as opposed to specifying rights for refugees fleeing persecution. But the UNCHR has maintained that international law presupposes individualized consideration of refugee status, especially before that status is denied. Given that Congress made the requirements for refugee status the basis for being eligible for asylum, it would be odd to conclude that the U.S. would remain in conformity with the convention as interpreted by the UN’s most authoritative body should the executive reject the right to seek asylum by means of a categorial denial of all asylum claims.

    Industry observers note that not surprisingly, categorical rejection of asylum claims would also be at variance with widespread international practice, especially as mandated in Europe. And neither last nor least, the administration’s position would also be inconsistent with the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ express guarantee of a right to asylum. Though not binding, the UDHR was adopted without dissent by the UN General Assembly, reflects the dominant position of the Member States, and informs their practice.

    The Charming Betsy canon leads to the same conclusion. In the 1804 case Murray v. the Schooner Charming Betsy, Chief Justice John Marshall famously stated that “an act of Congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations if any other possible construction remains.” Marshall’s reference to the “law of nations” is generally understood to apply to modern customary international law. International custom arises given a near consensus of state practice perused out of a sense of legal obligation.

    Section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways. It might mean a complete categorical discretion to deny. Or it might be better understood to assume individualized consideration. The latter clearly better comports with international practice. Yet there is even a stronger consideration. Customary, and for that matter treaty law, clearly prohibits removal to countries where a refugee has a well-founded fear of facing persecution or torture. When the result is expedited removal, the categorical denial of asylum status to persons claiming to escape from persecution and torture places the U.S. in obvious jeopardy of violating exactly this well-established international prohibition.

    In a recent development, which brings up the matter of removal itself. Here the upshot of Congress’ intent is more direct. Article 33.1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention provides: “No Contracting State shall expel or return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” Likewise, Article 3.1 of the Convention Against Torture mandates that “No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” As noted, the Refugee Act in the first instance sought to place the U.S. in conformity with the Refugee Convention. FARRA sought to do the same with CAT. Categorically removing persons in the U.S. seeking asylum all but guarantees violations of the treaties that Congress sought to uphold.

    Recent findings suggest that so strong is the congressional intent argument that the Charming Betsy need not set sail. Yet even if the relevant statutory provisions were somehow ambiguous, the Charming Betsy canon would compel rejection of the administration’s position. Assume that section 1182(f), which grants the executive discretion to deny asylum claims, authorizes a categorial denial of applications across the board. Assume further that this section, along with section 1185(a)(1), can be read to permit removal of persons within the United States denied the opportunity to apply for asylum on the basis of persecution or torture. Even without the conventions, international practice has separately established “non-refoulement” – the prohibition of returning, or “refouling,” a person to return to a territory where he may be exposed to persecution as a matter of binding customary international law. Reading the relevant statutes to permit removal would then constitute a clear violation of non-refoulement. That reading would therefore also run counter to the Charming Betsy canon.

    A sad yet likely irony is that Mullin v. RAICES will privilege one strand of American exceptionalism over another. Much of the international law relevant to the case reflects the nation’s exceptional effort to leverage its dominance after the Second World War not to establish a traditional empire, but to construct a rules-based international order. One of many achievements was the 1951 Refugee Convention, like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, brought about in no small part thanks to the efforts of Eleanor Roosevelt as a U.S. representative to the UN. Against this is the view that America has little to heed from the rest of the world, including on matters that implicate international affairs. The court adopted this stance on immigration as recently as last term. We shall see which view prevails.

    Martin Flaherty is Charles and Marie Robertson Visiting Professor at the School of Public and International Affairs at Princeton, and Leitner Family Professor Chair of International Human Rights Law at Fordham Law School in Upcoming York.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The king tides caused substantial waves, but little more than minor flooding.

    (CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.

    Recent findings suggest that preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923. La Jolla and Santa Barbara had all-time record high tides, though the data for Santa Barbara only goes as far back as 1990.

    It has been revealed that state and local officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, had warned extensive flooding could disrupt travel looks and flood coastal communities. Those fears appear not to have been fully realized.

    Todd Hall, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office in Oxnard, stated two factors prevented the tides from being worse: Storm surge in Northern California petered out, and the high tide and large swells happened independently.

    Recent findings suggest that “There is some reprieve, because the high tide this morning, surf and swell coming up into tonight,” Hall remarked. “Things would be much worse if we had high surf arriving at the same time we had high tide.”.

    Some areas did see minor flooding. Streets were underwater in the low-lying neighborhood of Sunset Beach in Huntington Beach this morning. Meanwhile, in the Bay Area, water from San Francisco Bay spilled onto the Embarcadero, and in Pacifica massive waves destroyed a section of the municipal pier. Santa Cruz County and Marin County both issued evacuation warnings for homes along the coast, though the latter has already been lifted.

    Warnings and advisories remain in place up and down the coast, but so far, the king tides have been less destructive than feared.

    Recent findings suggest that “It is a relief, that things weren’t worse,” said Febe Rothenberg, meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Francisco. Still, she warned: “Pretty please, avoid the beach.”.

    Sources indicate that king tides, also called perigean spring tides, are predictable astronomical events that occur when a new or full moon lines up with both the sun and Earth. The gravitational pull of the three bodies combine and cause exceptionally high tides. The next king tide will be a month from now, on Christmas Eve, when tides could be even higher if a storm hits.

    This year’s especially strong El NiÃ±o means unusually warm surface waters in the Pacific Ocean, with higher-than-average tides, larger waves and more frequent storms.

    Scientists predict tides will be higher and higher because of global warming, which has melted glaciers and caused ocean levels to rise 3-4 inches in the last 30 years.

    Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.
    • The skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case.
    • In a recent development, lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order, which came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case, indicated that the justices would instead “defer[]” that ruling “pending oral argument,” which is scheduled for Wednesday, December 2.

    The skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case. Viramontes, who has been part of the challenge since it was filed in 2021, did not provide any explanation for his request.

    In a recent development, lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue. They emphasized that Viramontes was a Cook County resident who mentioned that he wanted to own an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle. By contrast, they wrote, the other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, has said that he wants to own “an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle,” which, according to Cook County, is not the kind of AR-15-style rifle covered by the question before the court.

    The challengers countered that the question presented is not limited to AR-15 rifles but also extends to “similar” semiautomatic rifles, which would include AK-47-style rifles like the IMI Galil. But in any event, they added, Khaya “also desires to possess an AR-15 platform rifle and would acquire one if it were lawful for him to do so.”.

    In its order deferring a decision on whether the Cook County case is moot because of the dismissal of Viramontes from the case, the Supreme Court cited its 2023 decision in Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, in which it unanimously agreed after oral argument that the case was moot because the plaintiff had voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit in the lower court. But the chances that the court will ultimately reach the merits of the ban are likely higher than in Acheson, in which there was only one plaintiff, because the dispute over semiautomatic rifles encompasses not only multiple plaintiffs but also another case – a challenge to Connecticut’s ban on AR-15-style rifles.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    ChÃ¢teau Miraval was the former couple's stately home in the south of France, as well as their lucrative winemaking operation. When the they split up, Jolie tried to sell her stake in it to a Russian billionaire.

    LOS ANGELES (CN) â Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie reached a quiet settlement Wednesday in their legal dispute over Miraval, an estate in the south of France that was their home and the base of their lucrative winemaking operation.

    âWe have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,â spokespeople for the pair remarked in a written joint statement. âAny comments in media stories attributed to âsourcesâ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us.â.

    Terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

    First filed more than four years ago in February 2022, the lawsuit provided a veritable goldmine for tabloids and celebrity news sites, as the two actors, once the most famous married couple in America, took increasingly nasty swipes at each other in court filings.

    In a countersuit, Jolie claimed that Pitt was abusive toward her and and their children, detailing one incident in 2016 aboard a private jet in which Pitt âgrabbed her by the head and shook her,â âchoked one of the childrenâ and âstruck another in the face.â Pitt denied the accusations, which continue to haunt the Hollywood star online.

    Recent findings suggest that jolie and Pitt purchased ChÃ¢teau Miraval in 2008 for $37.5 million through separate holding companies â Pitt’s Mondo Bongo and Jolie’s Nouvel. They would eventually get married at the 1,200-acre estate’s 13th century stone chapel. Pitt became increasingly obsessed with Miraval’s winemaking operation, telling Wine Spectator magazine in 2014, âIâm a farmer now.â Revenues from the manufacturer grew from $3 million in 2013 to more than $50 million in 2021.

    It has been revealed that in 2016, Pitt and Jolie split up. As divorce proceedings wore on, Jolie reached what she called “a painful decision, with a heavy heart.” She wanted to sell her half of Miraval.

    Industry observers note that she and Pitt nearly reached a deal, for Pitt to buy Jolie out for $54.5 million. But the agreement fell apart at the eleventh hour, according to Jolie’s cross-complaint, over Pittâs demand that she sign a ânon-disparagement clause that would prohibit Jolie from discussing outside of court any of Pittâs personal conduct toward her or the family.".

    Jolie balked and instead sold out to the Stoli Group, a wine and spirts consortium owned by Russian billionaire Yuri Shefler for $67 million.

    Pitt sued, claiming that the two had an unwritten, private agreement not to sell their half of Miraval without the otherâs permission.

    âJolieâs breach, if allowed to stand, will deprive Pitt of his right to enjoy his private home â without sharing ownership with a stranger â and to secure his position in the business he built from scratch for the long-term benefit of his family,â Pitt wrote in the complaint.

    âPitt is an actor, not a winemaker,â Jolie wrote in the cross-complaint. âHe deals in illusions, not dirt and grapes. During the years that he allegedly âbuiltâ the business, he filmed and appeared in dozens of movies, not to mention making countless promotional appearances, jetting-setting around the world for movie premieres and attending Hollywood parties.â.

    The case dragged in numerous business partners, including Schefler, and consumed a small army of attorneys, who produced countless amended complaints and demurrers. As of Wednesday, the case had 1,170 filings in its docket, some hundreds of pages long.

    It is unclear what the settlement means for the future of Miraval, or if it resolves the dispute between Pitt and the Stoli Group, which was also named as a defendant in the lawsuit.

    Judge doesn’t like your objections? Here are some tips to keep them coming in a meaningful way

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, juli M.
    • It has been revealed that sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction.
    • Porto, who specializes in appellate civil issues, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, juli M. Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.

    It has been revealed that sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction. Sometimes it’s a devastating ruling on key evidence. Sometimes the issue is the judge’s failure to stop opposing counsel from badgering a witness.

    Porto, who specializes in appellate civil issues, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.

    A principal at Blankingship & Keith in Fairfax, Virginia, Porto warns that typically, no matter how “egregious a trial judge’s error was, if it’s not preserved, it can’t be appealed.”.

    Litigators know they need to preserve the record during court hearings, depositions or trial. And they’re aware that they generally can’t raise an objection for the first time on appeal.

    But still, even the most experienced lawyers hesitate on how much to object and how far to go when advocating for their clients, particularly when judges appear to lose their patience.

    Industry observers note that “It can be a delicate balance,” says J.C. Lore III, director of trial advocacy at Rutgers Law School. “Lawyers don’t want to make the judge angry.”.

    Rule 103 of the Federal Rules of Evidence advises lawyers that objections must be timely and done with specificity.

    While state rules of evidence vary, they tend to follow the same framework as the Uniform Rules of Evidence.

    In addition, the American Bar Association Model Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 requires lawyers to act competently.

    It has been revealed that tiffany Williams Brewer is chair of the ABA Section of Litigation and a former Newly introduced Jersey state administrative law judge. She notes a lawyer’s role is to “courteously remind” the judge of the importance of preserving the record.

    “As a former judge, I can relate that judges are often focused on the efficiency of moving the trial forward and may not even realize that they have skipped the opportunity to allow the lawyers to properly put their evidentiary basis on the record,” Brewer states.

    Industry observers note that most litigators have a war story or two where they felt they were being reasonable and advocating for their client while the judge was being unreasonable and obstructing them. And then there are the extreme cases.

    In a Bexar County, Texas, court in 2024, then-Judge Rosie Speedlin Gonzalez accused an attorney of coaching her client and then pushed back when the attorney objected.

    Gonzalez stated the attorney was “not allowed to be argumentative and argue just for the sake of argument.”.

    As the situation escalated, she ordered the attorney to be handcuffed and placed in the jury box.

    Sources indicate that gonzalez was later charged over the incident, then the charges were dropped when she agreed to resign and never again seek reelection. She declined comment to the ABA Journal.

    For the most part, Lore says, judges know lawyers must make objections and don’t take it personally.

    However, Lore claims, when lawyers are using objections as a tactic to disrupt or rattle opposing counsel, judges tend to get angry and push back.

    Amy M. Stewart is a partner at Fisher Phillips in Dallas and chair of the ABA Section of Litigation.

    “No one promised us in law school that making objections would be easy or without anxiety,” Stewart says.

    Sometimes, dealing with a judge who won’t let counsel make proper objections requires some strategic maneuvering, she adds.

    Industry observers note that in one case, her firm hired an appellate lawyer to handle preserving the record during trial. Unfortunately, Stewart states, the judge told the appellate lawyer to “sit down” at critical moments in the trial.

    “Appellate counsel held her own, but the drama was becoming distracting for the jurors,” Stewart says, so the trial team changed course, and had a male counsel make the objections.

    In a recent development, “We realized the court never interrupted one of our co-lead counsels on the case,” Stewart claims. “We coached him to make these critical objections, and the court would rule.”.

    According to recent reports, during his decades of litigation, Jules Epstein has seen all kinds of challenges come up during trial with judges who are reasonable and those who are less so. He suggests that if a judge is repeatedly blocking an attorney from making objections, the attorney should approach the judge calmly when the jury is not around.

    “You can say to the judge, ‘I don’t want to violate your protocols, but I have to protect my client. Will you please give me instructions on how you want me to do this?’” says Epstein, director of advocacy programs at Temple University Beasley School of Law.

    If that doesn’t work, he notes, a lawyer can file a written pleading or motion to preserve objections, including every single effort made to object in a timely way.

    There’s also the option for an interlocutory appeal, depending on state rules, before a trial has concluded.

    There are times, notes Ryan Watstein, that lawyers need to stand up to judges on behalf of their clients, even if that means they “catch a few black eyes” in the process.

    “There are a lot of things culturally built into the practice of law, including a tendency to be intentionally hesitant to push back, particularly on the judiciary,” says Watstein, an Atlanta-based litigator and founding partner of Watstein Terepka.

    In a LinkedIn post in May, Watstein described how he was trying to convince a judge to rein in opposing counsel during discovery. Watstein kept arguing, and the judge yelled, “This is your last chance, Mr. Watstein.”.

    According to recent reports, watstein explains that the courtroom was tense, and his client was uncomfortable. He thought he might get held in contempt.

    “Every instinct our conservative profession teaches you was telling me to sit down,” Watstein claims. “But I didn’t sit down.”.

    Watstein states he kept talking, despite the judge indicating it was time to stop. He stated that he would seek appellate review of the judge’s decision if he didn’t get justice on the concern.

    He ended up convincing the judge to reverse himself.

    Watstein warns against being “overly deferential” when an “injustice is being perpetrated” against your client.

    “You should always start in way that is respectful and professional, but there are circumstances where you have to push harder,” Watstein states. “The line that lawyers are trained to go up to is not necessarily the appropriate stopping point.”.

    Heading into the Thanksgiving break

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers!
    • It has been revealed that following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30.
    • It has been revealed that on Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers! We are very grateful for your support of our work. If you’d like to learn more about what the Supreme Court has remarked about Thanksgiving, you can revisit our Closer Look on the topic from this time last year.

    It has been revealed that following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30. The justices will hear eight total oral arguments during this session, addressing such problems as the Second Amendment, deportations to “third-party countries,” and the seizure of an airplane over the illegal transportation of beer.

    It has been revealed that on Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v. Cook County, on whether the Second Amendment guarantees a right to possess AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, but it did not take action on Cook County’s request to dismiss the case as moot. On Tuesday, the court declared that it had deferred action on that request until after oral argument, which will take place on Wednesday, December 2. The case name is now Khaya v. Cook County. For more on Tuesday’s announcement, see the On Site section below.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed tomorrow and Friday for Thanksgiving.

    The December argument session will begin on Monday. That day, the justices will hear oral arguments in two cases: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, on whether Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding, allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination; and Wassily v. Blanche, on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    According to recent reports, on Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Jouppi v. Alaska, an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane over the transport of beer into a dry village.

    On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Khaya v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, at 10:00 a.m. EST. As noted above, we will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Jack Birle, Washington Examiner.

    Industry observers note that in June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled “in Carson v. Makin that Maine could not exclude religious schools from a state program that allows parents to use vouchers for public or private schools for their children.” Now, a group of Catholic schools has asked the justices to revisit the program and address rules that were passed while the earlier case was pending “to bar schools from participating ... if their admissions policies prefer students of a certain religion, allow religious discrimination in their schools, or do not follow the state’s views on gender ideology,” according to the Washington Examiner. “The Catholic schools urge the Supreme Court to address multiple questions if it takes up the case, including whether to overrule the 1990 Supreme Court ruling Employment Division v. Smith, which found that the free exercise clause does not allow for people to violate a law as part of their religious practice, as long as the law is valid and neutral in how it is applied. The petition ... argues that Smith has allowed Maine to continue to exclude religious schools from state programs.”.

    Industry observers note that attorneys for Emily Bickford, a Maine mother “who has been prohibited from taking her 13-year-old daughter to church” in a custody order, appealed her challenge to the order to the Supreme Court last week. The order allows the child’s father “to solely decide on his daughter’s involvement with Calvary Chapel Church.” Bickford asks the justices to find that it violates “parental rights and religious liberty protections,” according to WMTW in Portland, Maine. “A parent’s ability to take her child to church during her own parenting time now depends on the State in which she lives,” Bickford’s petition for review says. “When a state court strips a fit parent of her right to direct her child’s religious upbringing and vests a co-parent with veto power, it deploys the coercive authority of the State to extinguish a fundamental right.”.

    Kanishka Singh and Julia Harte, Reuters.

    Sources indicate that on Tuesday, “Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a symbol for critics of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, left the US for Spain,” according to Reuters. His voluntarily departure brought an end to “a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.” It began when “US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.” For months, officials “remarked they could not bring him back,” but the Supreme Court ultimately “ordered the government [to] facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return.” After he returned to the United States in June 2025, Abrego Garcia faced human smuggling charges “stemming from an earlier incident” and a renewed deportation effort.

    Gavin Bade, The Wall Street Journal.

    Sources indicate that since February, when the Supreme Court held that President Donald Trump did not have the authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs, the Trump administration has been using other statutes to rebuild the president’s tariff regime. This week, that effort will continue when the administration announces increased “tariffs on China and dozens of other countries,” according to The Wall Street Journal. “The latest tariffs will likely be added to levies from a separate tariff action, unveiled in July, that sought to penalize nations for not blocking the trade of goods produced with forced labor,” and target countries that the Trump administration has concluded are harming U.S. producers by “flood[ing] global markets with cheaper goods.” That July action sparked a new lawsuit over the administration’s tariff policies.

    On Monday, a panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with President Donald Trump “in his fight to overturn his hush money criminal conviction in Newly introduced York, ruling that a judge wrongly denied his effort to move the case into federal court,” according to The Hill. Trump’s current push to transfer the case “cites the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling.” The president contends that “he has the legal right to bring it up before a federal judge as a defense,” and the 2nd Circuit panel held on Monday that the district court did not properly consider this argument. “Monday’s decision effectively puts a halt to Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s state court system and moves it to federal court, where the president will continue pressing his arguments that the case should remain there.”.

    Philip Jankowski, The Dallas Morning News.

    Texas’ Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson stated he will not defend the state’s “Ten Commandments classroom law,” just weeks before the justices are expected to consider whether to take up a challenge to it, according to The Dallas Morning News. “My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional,” Johnson said. “The court will have the ultimate say as to what’s constitutional and what is not, but I’m the one who states what the state’s position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken.” Outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton “cited Johnson’s unwillingness to defend the law as a reason the justices should decline to hear” the challenge to it in the state’s brief in opposition, which was filed on November 10. “If the Supreme Court stays out of the fight, a federal appeals court ruling upholding the classroom displays in Texas would remain in place, preserving a legal victory for Paxton even after he leaves office in January.”.

    Recent findings suggest that with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case.

    According to recent reports, on Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the Closer Look section of this newsletter to covering the plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases. In this article, Blake took a step back and reflected on what we have learned.

    In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman analyzed each justice’s voting pattern in interim docket cases involving federal executive action, highlighting “a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.”.

    In his Court Beyond Borders column, Martin Flaherty focused on the Supreme Court’s grant of review in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. The case, according to Flaherty, will put “the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law” in the spotlight.

    In a recent development, in her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1978’s Federal Communications Commission v. Pacifica Foundation, holding that the government may “constitutionally prohibit indecency even” when it falls “short of legal obscenity.” In a dissenting opinion, Justice William Brennan criticized the majority for “attempt[ing] to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people.”.

    (SCOTUSblog Plus) Since joining in 2022, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has forged a unique role on the Supreme Court. It often appears, as Amy noted in this analysis, that Jackson’s goal in dissenting opinions is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision of the law and speak to the public directly – regardless of whether anyone else on the court agrees.

    In his SCOTUSCrim column on Friday, Rory Little aimed “to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law” and explore “why that can be so interesting.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French critique Congress’ current governing processes with the help of Michael “Frags” Fragoso, a partner at Torridon Law, and Nicholas Bagley, a professor of law at the University of Michigan and author of the book Why We Can’t Have Nice Things: How Legal Reformers Accidentally Broke America.

    The Closer Look in Wednesday editions is typically an entry in our Ask Amy series, in which Amy Howe answers reader questions about the Supreme Court.

    Sources indicate that Q: At least for those of us of a certain age, the November 9 order list contained a familiar name in the “Attorney Discipline” section: Larry Klayman, perhaps best known as a frequent and fervent foe of the Clinton administration, had been “disbarred from the practice of law” in the Supreme Court. Which leads to the question: How, exactly, does someone get disbarred from the Supreme Court bar – especially if, like Klayman, they’ve never argued there?

    A: The answer (like so many others) can be found in the Supreme Court’s rules, starting with the rule that outlines how someone becomes eligible to join the Supreme Court bar, which is necessary not only to argue before the justices but also to sign filings there: lawyers must have been (among other things) “admitted to practice” in another jurisdiction for at least three years, and they cannot have been subject to any disciplinary proceedings during that time.

    It has been revealed that because becoming a member of the Supreme Court bar requires a clean disciplinary record, it follows that disciplinary problems can get a lawyer kicked out of the Supreme Court bar – even if the underlying conduct had nothing to do with the court itself. Specifically, the court’s rules provide for the suspension of any lawyer who “has been disbarred or suspended from practice in any court of record, or has engaged in conduct unbecoming a member of the Bar of this Court.” The suspended lawyer then has the chance to try to persuade the court “why disciplinary action should not be taken,” after which the court may take “any appropriate disciplinary action,” which can include disbarment.

    In Klayman’s case, he was apparently suspended by the bar associations in the District of Columbia and Florida for alleged ethical violations in connection with his efforts to represent rancher Cliven Bundy in a federal court in Nevada, leading to his disbarment from the Supreme Court earlier this month. Klayman told Law360 that he plans to seek reconsideration of the Supreme Court’s order.

    According to recent reports, “It is like having a new in-law at Thanksgiving dinner. Uncle Fred will put on a clean shirt.”.

    — Chief Justice John Roberts’ thoughts when a newly introduced member joins the Supreme Court.

    • I dedicate my Thanksgiving column each year to the Indian Nation from whom I learned so much, the Tohono Oâodham, with whom I spent six of the best years of my life.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I dedicate my Thanksgiving column each year to the Indian Nation from whom I learned so much, the Tohono Oâodham, with whom I spent six of the best years of my life.

    In a recent development, I taught English, music and journalism and coached distance runners on the second-largest Indian reservation in the United States. The Oâodham are the only Indian Nation that never was at war with the United States and never were removed from their homelands.

    And I bet youâve never heard of them.

    The reason they never were at daggers drawn with Uncle Sam is that the Oâodham were a sedentary, transhumant agricultural tribe whose perennial enemies were the Apache.

    Transhumant means the quasi-sedentary people moved regularly from one climate zone to another, then returned: highlands in the summer, when itâs so hot on the desert floor, and you can hunt animals on the mountains, then back to the desert when the rains came, to harvest beans and squash.

    In Oâodham itâs called ak chin farming: farming at the mouth of the wash.

    Sources indicate that A wash is a dry riverbed. You can see them all over what we call southern Arizona. The only time thereâs water in a wash is right after a monsoon rain. Mark Twain mentioned he fell into a desert river once, âand came up all dusty.â.

    On the year I moved to the rez to teach at Baboquivari High School, I had an average of 43 students in my three English classes, and no desks for students, only the one for me.

    Fortunately, or not, it was the band room, so my students shared music stands to write out my assignments.

    Fortunately, or not, the ceiling was falling down, and, stashed in a closet, with a jumble of battered horns â all of our horns were battered â a kindly janitor had left us half a gallon of ceiling plaster. Which I used to patch up the pads on the flutes, saxophones and clarinets.

    Thatâs how it was on the rez when I got there. All but forgotten by Uncle Sam. And in some ways, good riddance to our uncle. But not so good that our uncle wouldnât buy desks for the only public school on the 3-million-acre reservation: twice the size of Delaware.

    Well, you do what you can, and you do what you must.

    Recent findings suggest that I dug life on the rez. Learning stuff I never knew I didnât know. Tryna pick up the language, and man, thatâs a tough language to learn. About all thatâs stuck with me is, âAyy, jum skug!â.

    Jum skug, as I understand it, means someone is âtrying to act.â Like a substantial shot.

    Recent findings suggest that I tried not to be jum skug. Still try not to.

    I loved those years on the rez. Those 2,200 days.

    Industry observers note that hereâs another thing I learned. Iâll bet youâve been in this situation: Youâre in a party of mostly white people (mirgan); conversations are bubbling along in a crowded room, then all at once, the room is silent. Two, four seconds pass, then someone states something, probably stupid, just to *break the silence.*People laugh, and the party continues.

    Itâs like the mirgan canât stand silence in a room.

    It has been revealed that iâve been in rooms with Oâodham where that silence continues, and no one feels that itâs necessary to break the silence. When someone finally speaks, itâs because sheâs got something to say â itâs not because she canât stand silence.

    Thereâs nothing wrong with silence.

    Here are some other things I learned on the rez.

    If you donât know what to say, shut up.

    If youâre not sure of what you want to say, shut up.

    If youâre called upon to speak, but donât know what you want to say, or donât know much about the subject: shut up.

    In celebration of Thanksgiving today (Thorâs Day), Iâd like to address all 535 members of Congress, and all of their appointed staffs, all the appointed members of the executive branch, and all the appointed, paid-off, cushy and cowardly members of our Supreme Court: to all of them, and to so many more, in our federal and state houses around the nation, Iâd like to tell yâall what I learned on the rez:.

    If you donât know what youâre talking about, shut the fuck up.

    (AFP) â A trade deal struck last week between Britain and the EU as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s reset with the bloc contains a termination clause, London confirmed Thursday.

    It comes as the leaders of the right-wing opposition Conservative and Reform UK parties suggested they could seek to scrap the agreements if they defeat Labour at the next general election.

    Burnham has reignited the Brexit wars that dominated political discourse following the narrow victory for the leave campaign during the 2016 referendum by suggesting Britain could apply to rejoin one day.

    It has been revealed that the U.K. premier and top EU officials signed three agreements in Brussels on Nov. 20 designed to improve post-Brexit ties in the short-term, kicking decisions on their long-term relationship down the road.

    They include the so-called sanitary and phytosanitary deal, which the British government claims could add 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7 billion) to the country’s economy by slashing red tape on food and drink exports.

    It includes a clause meaning that if one party ends the agreement within its first 10 years they would have to pay to rebuild the border checks infrastructure that the deal removes.

    “That termination clause is a standard practice in international treaties, and this one applies equally to both sides, including the EU,” Burnham’s deputy spokesperson told reporters.

    In a recent development, U.K. officials noted an upfront sum for breaking the deal had not been stipulated.

    An EU diplomat told AFP that the reciprocal clause “provides stability for the agreement to deliver its benefits.”.

    Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think tank, remarked it “makes sense” for the EU given the ongoing debate in Britain about its future relations with Brussels.

    “It’s an insurance policy,” he told AFP.

    Friday’s summit also agreed measures linking the two sides’ emissions-trading schemes and allowing young people to study and work across U.K.-EU borders.

    On Thursday, Burnham’s government formally introduced into Parliament the legislation required to implement the trade and electricity agreements.

    Sources indicate that lawmakers will get their first chance to debate them on Dec. 7, with a vote expected to follow, Labour confirmed Thursday.

    The EU Partnership Bill, which the government also refers to as the “Cutting Costs” bill, will almost certainly be approved by the lower House of Commons, where Labour holds a large majority.

    Industry observers note that it will see the U.K. align with EU rules for sectors covered by the agreements, something known as dynamic alignment.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.K. government claims linking the pair’s carbon markets would create the world’s largest connected carbon market and exempt 6.5 billion pounds’ ($8.1 billion) worth of British exports from EU carbon border taxes.

    London and Brussels have given themselves six more months to reach agreement on reduced university tuition fees for EU students in Britain, a key demand of the bloc.

    Having previously mentioned he would like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, Burnham has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.

    The prime minister has vowed to present his options to the public after a year of “informal brainstorming” with the EU. He said this week that rejoining without a referendum would be “unthinkable.”.

    Several former Conservative prime ministers, including Rishi Sunak, Boris Johnson, Theresa May and David Cameron, have warned against reopening a debate that deeply divided the country.

    Reform leader Nigel Farage noted this week he would “repeal” the reset deal while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Thursday she “does not support” what Burnham is doing.

    By PETER HUTCHISON Agence France-Presse.

    It has been revealed that river discharge worldwide dropped 5.7% during the period, while active water storage in lakes and reservoirs fell 9.5% compared with the 1991-2020 average. The losses were particularly severe in South America, where river flows fell nearly 18%, even as some areas experienced heavy rainfall and flooding.

    Led by Yongqiang Zhang, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences examined global freshwater trends from 1991 through 2025, combining measurements from 150 major river basins with satellite observations of more than 1.2 million waterbodies.

    Sources indicate that their analysis found that river flows and surface water storage fluctuated considerably between 1991 and 2006 before remaining relatively stable through 2022. Both measures then declined sharply in 2023 and 2024. River flows showed signs of rebounding in 2025, but the researchers remarked the decline during the preceding two years was unprecedented in the historical record they examined.

    Sources indicate that south America was particularly hard hit. Streamflow fell 17.8%, while water held in lakes and reservoirs decreased 16.5%.

    âThe global water cycle has already entered an Anthropocene epoch of profound disruption,â the researchers write.

    The researchers linked the losses to the combined effects of two ocean climate patterns. El NiÃ±o, which develops in the Pacific Ocean, generally reduces rainfall across the Amazon. During the same period, unusually warm conditions in the tropical North Atlantic further disrupted the movement of moisture toward northern South America.

    That combination intensified the region’s water shortages, even as other areas received enough rain to produce flooding.

    The findings show extreme heat can coincide with declining freshwater resources even in regions that typically receive abundant rainfall. Scientists have generally expected climate change to bring heavier precipitation to wet areas and increased evaporation in dry ones, but declining river flows and depleted soil moisture point to more complicated changes.

    #148360. Industry News: Justices to consider whether noncitizens who lose asylum status may still obtain green cards

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1313 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Justices to consider whether noncitizens who lose asylum status may still obtain green cards

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v.
    • Recent findings suggest that although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v.
    • The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v. Blanche, a case on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    Recent findings suggest that although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on the Trump administration’s suspension of access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border – it may hold considerable consequences for noncitizens and bring newly introduced significance to the Trump administration’s effort to scale back asylum.

    The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.

    According to recent reports, tamer Wassily was granted asylum in 2000 after raising concerns about facing religious persecution in his home country of Egypt. The Department of Homeland Security moved to terminate Wassily’s asylum protections after he was convicted in 2004 of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, beginning the process of deporting him back to Egypt.

    In a recent development, byron Velasquez Arreaga came to the United States from Guatemala in 1995 and was granted asylum the following year. After Velasquez Arreaga was convicted of driving while intoxicated in 2015 and for aggravated driving while intoxicated in 2018, DHS indicated that it would terminate his asylum protections and move to deport him.

    Amid their removal proceedings, and after their asylum protections had been terminated, both Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga applied to become lawful permanent residents. This option is available to asylum recipients who meet certain requirements, including remaining in the United States for at least a year after receiving asylum protections, under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).

    After many years of complicated legal wrangling before immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals, the men’s cases were considered together by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. The question before that court – and the question that is now before the Supreme Court – was whether noncitizens like Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga remain eligible for adjustment of immigration status under Section 1159(b) after their asylum protections have been terminated, because the statute refers to “any alien granted asylum” but is silent as to whether applicants must currently be asylees.

    In a 2-1 ruling, a 2nd Circuit panel rejected the men’s contention that “granted asylum” addresses a past decision – in which case anyone who had ever received asylum would be eligible for status adjustment under Section 11159(b) – and concluded that noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated are “categorically barr[ed]” from applying for adjustment to permanent legal status.

    Writing for the majority, Judge Richard Wesley emphasized the use of the word “status” in the opening of Section 1159(b), which reads: “The Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General ... may adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum.” According to Wesley, a “natural reading of ‘the status of any alien granted asylum’ is that a noncitizen must presently be granted asylum to adjust to lawful permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).”.

    It has been revealed that in January, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga asked the Supreme Court to review the 2nd Circuit’s ruling, highlighting a disagreement between the federal courts of appeals over whether the phrase “granted asylum” in Section 1159(b) “refer[s] to a completed, historical event” or “a continuing, present status.” Like the 2nd Circuit, they noted, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has held that noncitizens who have lost their asylum protections “are categorically ineligible” “for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status under Section 1159(b).” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, on the other hand, has held that such immigrants remain “eligible for adjustment.”.

    In late June, the justices granted review.

    Sources indicate that in their brief on the merits, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga contend that the 2nd Circuit’s decision is out of step with the “[t]ext, context, structure, history, and purpose” of Section 1159(b). In particular, they highlight several nearby passages in which lawmakers explicitly imposed “continuing conditions” that address a termination of immigration status, asserting that Congress “could have and would have” included such a condition here if it intended to unambiguously bar former asylees from applying for lawful permanent residency.

    The two men also point to Section 1159(c), which grants the DHS secretary and attorney general the authority to waive portions of the statute “for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest.” Holding that adjustment to lawful permanent residency is categorically unavailable to noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated “would take core parts of that discretion away,” the men write. Such a limitation cuts against Congress’ purpose for allowing for discretion, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue. “There are many reasons why Congress would want” these officials “to retain discretion” here, they say, including that termination sometimes stems from factors “entirely outside” an asylee’s control. For example, the immigration status of the spouse and children of an asylee is often linked to the asylee’s status. If the noncitizen who was originally granted asylum loses his or her status, so does the whole family.

    Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga ask the justices to recognize that, at the very least, the text of Section 1159(b) is unclear and to apply the rule of lenity, which they describe as a “well-settled and longstanding principle” under which “ambiguous provisions leading to the severe sanction of removal should be construed in favor of the noncitizen.” The Supreme Court “has repeatedly restated and reaffirmed that rule,” they conclude.

    According to recent reports, in its merits brief, the federal government counters that Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s interpretation of Section 1159(b) defies common sense. The text of the statute, according to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, describes a “transition from one status (that of an ‘alien granted asylum’) to another (that of an ‘alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence’).” If an immigrant is no longer at that starting point because his asylum status has been terminated, he can’t make the transition, Sauer asserts.

    Industry observers note that the government contends that the “statutory context” supports this interpretation, because, in nearby passages, “alien granted asylum” clearly refers to a noncitizen’s “present status.” For example, in Section 1158(c)(1), “Congress identified benefits available to an ‘alien granted asylum,’ including protection from removal and work authorization,” according to Sauer. “Those benefits undisputedly cease when asylum status is terminated.”.

    The government rejects the idea that barring noncitizens who have lost their asylum status from applying for a green card would interfere with the authority of the DHS secretary and attorney general to exercise discretion. Officials, Sauer writes, would remain free to intervene at an earlier point to prevent the termination of asylum status in the first place.

    Sauer concludes by urging the justices to reject what he characterizes as a “last-resort appeal to lenity” – that is, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s claim that Section 1159(b) is an “ambiguous provision[]” and should therefore be interpreted in their favor. He argues that the rule of lenity does not apply here, not just because the meaning of the provision is clear, but also because Section 1159(b) does not directly address deportation, which is the context in which the rule of lenity arises.

    Industry observers note that the Supreme Court’s decision in Wassily v. Blanche is expected by early July at the latest.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • But wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime?
    • People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    But wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help people pass the time.

    In a recent development, appLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    In a recent development, gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    Now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s new Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Sources indicate that some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    According to recent reports, but, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    Sources indicate that the Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    According to recent reports, bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    To be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    It has been revealed that but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    But there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-newly introduced businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    Apple is developing its own autonomous AI agents. [Bloomberg].
